paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery in 2027?
Board discussion document, January 2027
Parcelbird
Board (two founders, two investors)
Board confidential; synthetic benchmark data from the briefing pack
Executive summary
Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: it loses money on every order and breaks the runway rule; sell fast-delivery software to grocers instead
Quick commerce is growing fast, but its operators lose money on every order
–	US sales reached $5.1B in 2025, 2.8 times the 2022 level
–	Zipcart loses $1.90 and QuickBasket $3.40 on each order
A dark store loses money at every level reached so far, and pop-up customers did not stay
–	The median customer site loses $6.17 per order, the best site $1.76
–	Only the founders' plan, above the best site on four inputs, is positive
–	Only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three
The launch breaks the 12-month runway rule, with no new funding in sight
–	The plan plus today's burn leaves cash $4.7M short by month 18
–	Even the kindest reading leaves about 6 months of runway at month 18
Selling fast-delivery software to grocers captures the same demand for $1.2M
–	Late-stage grocers would add $864K a year, 21% of today's ARR
–	A one-store pilot would cost $3.6M to retest what we already know

slides.title: At the median customer site, a dark store loses $6.17 on every order, with rider cost the largest drain

paragraphs.text: 1 Market    2 Unit economics    3 Cash    4 Alternative
At the median customer site, a dark store loses $6.17 on every order, with rider cost the largest drain
Contribution per order at the benchmark median site, $ per order, 14 customer sites, 2025
The loss is built in before the store pays rent
▪	Rider cost: at 2.4 orders an hour, rider time takes 81% of the margin earned on the goods
▪	Rider pay rules: two of the three launch cities are considering minimum pay for delivery workers, which would raise the largest cost further
▪	Promotions: discounts at 6% of the order cost more than the delivery fee brings in
▪	Site fixed cost: the order is negative even before it, so more orders per site cannot close the gap alone
1  Margin on goods = $34 average order × 27%; rider cost = $17.75 an hour ÷ 2.4 orders; site fixed cost = $1.15M a year ÷ (900 orders × 365 days)
Sources: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

The plan's profit sits outside anything observed

▪	Columbus pop-up: our own test lost about twice as much per order as the median site
▪	What would flip it: at the best site's order value and density, riders would need 4.3 orders an hour to break even

slides.title: The launch breaks the runway rule: with today's burn added, cash would be $4.7M short by month 18

paragraphs.text: 1 Market    2 Unit economics    3 Cash    4 Alternative
The launch breaks the runway rule: with today's burn added, cash would be $4.7M short by month 18
Parcelbird cash, $ millions, today to month 18 of the launch plan
Every dollar of the plan breaks the floor
▪	Without the launch: today's burn alone brings cash to $4.8M by month 18, exactly the 12-month floor
▪	Kindest reading: if the plan's figure already covers today's burn, cash at month 18 lasts about 6 months, half the minimum
▪	No new money: the lead investor calls a round for a delivery operator unlikely, so the plan must fit today's cash
▪	Plan losses are the optimistic case: at the economics customer sites actually reach, operating losses would be larger
Any 2027 plan must lower the burn, not add to it
1  Plan cash covers capex for 9 dark stores at $0.6M each, launch marketing and operating losses; today's burn of $0.4M a month is held flat for 18 months
Sources: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis
